```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
  fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 150, fig.path = "figures/"
)
```

Real datasets rarely arrive ready to analyze. This report takes the **World Health Organization (WHO) tuberculosis dataset**, a classic example of messy data, and reshapes it step by step into a **tidy** format with `tidyr` and `dplyr`. It then shows why the effort pays off: once the data is tidy, summaries and plots take only a few lines.

```{r libraries}
library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))
```

## 1. What is tidy data?

A dataset is **tidy** when:

1. Each **variable** is a column.
2. Each **observation** is a row.
3. Each **value** is a cell.

## 2. The raw data

The data comes from the WHO *Global Tuberculosis Report* and is included in `tidyr` as `who`. It records tuberculosis cases by country, year, diagnosis method, sex and age group.

```{r raw}
who
dim(who)
```

The dataset has **`r ncol(who)` columns**, but only a few of them are real variables:

- `country`, `iso2` and `iso3` all identify the country, so two of them are redundant.
- `year` is a variable.
- The other `r ncol(who) - 4` columns, from `new_sp_m014` to `newrel_f65`, are **not variables**: their names combine several pieces of information (diagnosis, sex and age), and their cells hold the number of cases.

## 3. Step by step

### Step 1 · Gather the case columns into rows

All the case columns are stacked into two: `key` (the old column name) and `cases` (the count). Most cells are empty, so `values_drop_na = TRUE` removes them.

```{r step1}
who1 <- who |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = new_sp_m014:newrel_f65,
    names_to = "key",
    values_to = "cases",
    values_drop_na = TRUE
  )

who1
```

Counting the keys shows the structure of the codes:

```{r keys}
who1 |> count(key)
```

### Step 2 · Understand the codes

Each key follows the pattern `new_<type>_<sex><age>`:

| Part | Values | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Prefix | `new` | New tuberculosis cases (every column in this dataset) |
| Type | `sp` | Pulmonary, smear-positive: detected with a sputum smear test |
| | `sn` | Pulmonary, smear-negative: not detected with a smear test |
| | `ep` | Extrapulmonary: outside the lungs |
| | `rel` | Relapse: a patient who had tuberculosis before |
| Sex | `m` / `f` | Male / female |
| Age group | `014`, `1524`, `2534`, `3544`, `4554`, `5564`, `65` | 0–14, 15–24, 25–34, 35–44, 45–54, 55–64 and 65+ years |

### Step 3 · Fix the inconsistent names

The relapse columns are written `newrel` instead of `new_rel`. If this is not fixed, the next step splits them incorrectly.

```{r step3}
who2 <- who1 |>
  mutate(key = str_replace(key, "newrel", "new_rel"))

who2 |> filter(str_detect(key, "rel")) |> distinct(key) |> head()
```

### Step 4 · Split the key into its parts

The key is split at each `_` into three columns.

```{r step4}
who3 <- who2 |>
  separate_wider_delim(key, delim = "_", names = c("new", "type", "sexage"))

who3
```

### Step 5 · Drop redundant columns

`new` has the same value in every row, and `iso2` and `iso3` repeat `country`.

```{r step5}
who3 |> count(new)

who4 <- who3 |>
  select(-new, -iso2, -iso3)
```

### Step 6 · Separate sex and age

The first character is the sex and the rest is the age group.

```{r step6}
who5 <- who4 |>
  separate_wider_regex(sexage, patterns = c(sex = "[mf]", age = ".*"))

who5
```

### Step 7 · Make the values readable

```{r step7}
age_labels <- c("014" = "0–14", "1524" = "15–24", "2534" = "25–34", "3544" = "35–44",
                "4554" = "45–54", "5564" = "55–64", "65" = "65+")

type_labels <- c(sp = "Smear-positive", sn = "Smear-negative",
                 ep = "Extrapulmonary", rel = "Relapse")

who_tidy <- who5 |>
  mutate(
    type = factor(type_labels[type], levels = type_labels),
    sex  = factor(sex, levels = c("f", "m"), labels = c("Female", "Male")),
    age  = factor(age_labels[age], levels = age_labels)
  )

who_tidy
```

### All steps in one pipeline

```{r pipeline}
who_tidy_pipeline <- who |>
  pivot_longer(new_sp_m014:newrel_f65, names_to = "key",
               values_to = "cases", values_drop_na = TRUE) |>
  mutate(key = str_replace(key, "newrel", "new_rel")) |>
  separate_wider_delim(key, delim = "_", names = c("new", "type", "sexage")) |>
  select(-new, -iso2, -iso3) |>
  separate_wider_regex(sexage, patterns = c(sex = "[mf]", age = ".*"))

# Same result as the step-by-step version
nrow(who_tidy_pipeline) == nrow(who5)
```

## 4. Before and after

```{r before-after}
tibble(
  dataset = c("Raw (who)", "Tidy (who_tidy)"),
  rows    = c(nrow(who), nrow(who_tidy)),
  columns = c(ncol(who), ncol(who_tidy))
) |> kable(format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

From a wide table with `r ncol(who)` columns to a long table with `r ncol(who_tidy)` columns, one row per country, year, type, sex and age group.

## 5. Why it pays off: exploring the tidy data

> **Note:** reporting practices changed over time (for example, relapse cases only appear in the most recent years), so totals across years reflect **reported** cases, not true incidence.

### Reported cases over time

```{r cases-year}
who_tidy |>
  filter(year >= 1995) |>
  group_by(year, sex) |>
  summarise(cases = sum(cases), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(year, cases / 1e6, color = sex)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 1.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Female = "#D55E00", Male = "#0072B2")) +
  labs(title = "Reported new tuberculosis cases by sex",
       x = NULL, y = "Cases (millions)", color = NULL)
```

```{r male-share}
male_share <- who_tidy |>
  group_by(sex) |>
  summarise(cases = sum(cases)) |>
  mutate(share = cases / sum(cases)) |>
  filter(sex == "Male") |>
  pull(share)
```

Men account for **`r round(male_share * 100)`%** of all reported cases in the dataset.

### Cases by age group and sex

```{r cases-age}
who_tidy |>
  group_by(age, sex) |>
  summarise(cases = sum(cases), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(age, cases / 1e6, fill = sex)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), width = 0.7) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Female = "#D55E00", Male = "#0072B2")) +
  labs(title = "Reported cases by age group",
       x = "Age group (years)", y = "Cases (millions)", fill = NULL)
```

### Countries with the most reported cases

```{r top-countries, fig.height = 5}
top_countries <- who_tidy |>
  group_by(country) |>
  summarise(cases = sum(cases)) |>
  slice_max(cases, n = 10)

top_countries |>
  ggplot(aes(cases / 1e6, fct_reorder(country, cases))) +
  geom_col(fill = "#0072B2") +
  labs(title = "Top 10 countries by reported cases",
       x = "Cases (millions)", y = NULL)
```

```{r top-share}
top_share <- sum(top_countries$cases) / sum(who_tidy$cases)
```

The 10 countries with the most reported cases account for **`r round(top_share * 100)`%** of all cases in the dataset.

## Key takeaways

- Column names can hide several variables at once; `pivot_longer()` and the `separate_wider_*()` functions turn them back into proper columns.
- Small inconsistencies (`newrel` vs. `new_rel`) must be fixed **before** splitting, or the result is silently wrong.
- Once the data is tidy, every summary above is just `group_by()` + `summarise()` + `ggplot()`.
